name: Beth Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a candle-pouring machine and check the first jar after every wax or fragrance change. I came from a bakery, so I am still a junior learning this line at fifty-eight with secondary schooling. Night premiums lift my pay above the usual operator rate, and I like seeing a clean rack leave the machine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and how do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Omar repairs cars at a garage, and our grown children have homes of their own. We have a housing loan, about ten months saved and plenty of similar packaging plants nearby. I use AI every day to group spills and delivery delays, but I still check the batch sheet before changing a setting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the candle crew that a little AI help with orders is fine. A wax-pouring machine still needs someone to check the first jar for a crooked wick and an even fill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am new to the pouring line after years at a bakery, and the senior operator checks my first setup. Night premiums make the wage good for this job, while Omar’s garage pay and our ten-month reserve cover the house with our grown children away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid night shift and measure the first jars after a fragrance change. I would keep using my daily AI log to group spills and stoppages, then put fresh full-month wages toward our housing loan after bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be calm about current work. A quiet factory year would let us enjoy Sunday lunch without checking the phone for roster news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why measure a jar?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A crooked wick burns into the glass, and an overfill wastes wax. I check the first run and call the setter before a whole rack is spoiled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does AI do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It groups my notes on spills and late fragrance deliveries. I still check the paper batch sheet before changing a setting.

I would keep **first-jar checks** on the pouring line after every fragrance change.
think: My **night premium** lifts this junior wage above the usual operator rate.
Omar’s **garage pay** and ten months saved cover ordinary household setbacks.
do: Keep **night pouring shifts** and measure first jars.
Use the **existing daily AI log** for spills.
Pay extra **housing-loan principal** from fresh full-month wages.
feel: **Calm** about current work and a strong reserve.

fieldNote: Beth is **junior after bakery work**, despite her age and higher premium pay.
Her **ten-month reserve** and two incomes support calm, while extra debt payment uses newly earned wages.

steps.text: Keep night pouring shifts and check first jars

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the manager that scheduling software can be tried quickly, but any robot jar loader needs a guarded test. Good employers train their own people before cutting a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A camera might take the easy fill checks I do now, and a loader might later take another pair of hands. I am still junior on this line, so my own hours could be cut even with strong savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for an offered paid guarded trial on thirty jars with the setter beside me. If approved, I would learn the new AI fill threshold on test batches and compare it with hand measures; after a real hours cut, I would apply for posted reachable packaging work only where net pay after travel covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about my own rota, but I would rather test the jars than guess. A full account is no use if the factory stops paying me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks safety on the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The setter would isolate the loader and confirm the guard before I change a threshold. I would need an actual paid slot, not just a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a different shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it fits Omar’s garage hours and leaves us enough after travel. There are other packaging plants nearby, but a posting is not a job offer.

I would defend **paid operator training** at the plant.

feel: **Anxious** about a plausible loss of her own night shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AGI might arrive in 2028 when I am sixty, while robots able to handle hot jars follow around 2031 when I am sixty-three. Planning changes first; pouring work follows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the plant could remove my junior pouring shift when robots load and inspect jars. Our ten-month reserve and several nearby factories buy time, but Omar’s garage wage alone may not carry the housing loan for a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would postpone the planned bathroom rebuild and ask for written staffing dates. If my paid shift ends, I would apply for posted reachable packaging work only if net pay after travel covers our bills; if no adequate place appears, I would ask the lender about temporary terms before arrears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about possible wage loss but able to search. I would rather compare real openings than count years to a pension I have not priced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop work at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if actual retirement income and Omar’s confirmed pay cover housing, food and repairs. The reserve is not a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your grown children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own households. I would ask for a lift to an interview if it fits, not assume they can pay our loan.

I would ask for **written staffing dates** before physical cuts.
think: My **junior pouring shift** could go after capable robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AGI in 2031 finds me sixty-three and capable pouring robots around 2034 find me sixty-six. Five years gives an employer time to offer real paid apprenticeship places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the first-jar checks but am still learning line settings. I could move into machine care if a local plant posts the work, though I need a recognised qualification and safe practical instruction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the pouring shift and pay fresh full-month surplus against our housing loan. If the plant offers a funded paid-time maintenance course with an actual isolated pouring-machine place and a posted reachable role at bill-covering net pay, I would enrol; after qualifying I would apply for that job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious but able to compare a real wage with course time. I want to repair a stopped machine beside a fitter before anyone calls me qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your employer offer that place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask first; nothing is promised. A qualified fitter would isolate the hot feed and supervise my first repair if the plant actually offers the paid slot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course has no local job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my shift and compare posted operator openings if hours fall. I would not buy training simply because a brochure says demand is coming.

say: I would ask for **paid machine-care places** before 2034 robots.
I would seek **posted local wages** before enrolling.
think: My **junior skill** needs supervised practical repairs before I could qualify.
The **housing loan** still needs steady factory income at sixty-six.
do: Keep **pouring shifts** and pay extra housing loan from new wages.

feel: **Anxious**, with time to compare real course and job terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our church group that thinking AGI in 2036 finds me sixty-eight and capable robots around 2039 find me seventy-one. Ten years lets families check real work and retirement figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Omar and I hope to stop full-time work around sixty-seven, before the 2036 thinking-AI date, but I have not seen figures that prove we can. Our grown children have their own bills; they cannot be our reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the pouring shift and pay fresh surplus against our housing loan. I would request retirement and loan figures; if those show income enough for housing, food and repairs, I would stop factory work at our planned age sixty-seven, and in the first year after 2036 I would only check factory rosters if I am still employed because the figures fell short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about distant robots, with current wages and savings giving us room to decide. A planned last shift needs numbers behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the figures fall short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep safe paid work and check posted local jobs if the plant cuts my hours. I would not retire on a calendar while the loan still needs payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you teach your children the AI log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They are adults making their own work choices. I would show them the machine and the wage slip if they asked, not tell them which trade to take.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable jar robots around 2031 could cut my junior shift while our loan still needs wages. Written staffing dates, paid safe training and posted reachable work at bill-covering net pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the first jar before a family lights the candle. I like a good machine, but somebody has to own that first check.

headlineQuote: I like a good machine, but somebody has to own that first check.
portrait: **Beth**, 58, is a junior candle-pouring operator after a late move from bakery work, with secondary schooling and developing line skill.
Her **garage-worker partner**, grown children, housing loan, premium wage, ten-month reserve and many nearby plants provide options.
She uses **AI daily** for logs and would learn new vision settings only through offered paid guarded trials.
Fast robots threaten **pouring shifts** at sixty-three; her age-sixty-seven exit depends on verified retirement income.
biggestWorry: **Fast physical robots** could cut her junior pouring shift around 2031 before the planned income-based retirement point.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, offered funded safe instruction and posted reachable work at bill-covering net pay would help.
